children.alt: Side-by-side boxplots of Exam 1 score for five declared majors -- Business, Kinesiology, Nursing, Other, and STEM. Medians range narrowly from about 56 to 63 points with heavily overlapping interquartile ranges across all five groups; Kinesiology has two high outlier points near 84 and 86.

children.value: Exam 1 score by declared major area — EDA before the ANOVA test.

Five means, all sitting within about six points of each other (58.8 to
64.4), with heavily overlapping boxes — EDA alone doesn’t show an obvious
winner or loser. That’s exactly the situation a formal test is for: is that
six-point spread more than you’d expect from sampling variability alone, or
is it a real difference?

. Four terms describe how such an experiment is
built:
The variable a researcher deliberately manipulates (e.g., which fertilizer a plant receives).
The specific values/categories the factor takes (e.g., Control, Treatment A, Treatment B).
, so no hidden variable systematically favors one level (e.g., shuffling which tree gets which fertilizer, instead of choosing by hand).
Measuring more than one unit per level, so you can tell a real effect from one unusually high or low measurement.

set.seed(2200)
fert_yield <- data.frame(
  fertilizer = factor(rep(c("Control", "Treatment A", "Treatment B"), each = 8),
                       levels = c("Control", "Treatment A", "Treatment B")),
  yield_lb   = round(c(rnorm(8, mean = 28, sd = 3),
                        rnorm(8, mean = 33, sd = 3),
                        rnorm(8, mean = 31, sd = 3)), 1)
)
favstats(yield_lb ~ fertilizer, data = fert_yield)

children.alt: Side-by-side boxplots of simulated almond yield in pounds per tree for three fertilizer treatments, 8 simulated trees each. Control has the lowest median around 28.5 pounds; Treatment A and Treatment B have higher medians near 32 to 33 pounds, with Treatment A showing the widest spread of the three groups.
